task_context.problem_statement:
Danny collects bottle caps and wrappers. He found 10 bottle caps and 62 wrappers at the park. Now he has 27 bottle caps and 43 wrappers in his collection.
How many more wrappers than bottle caps does danny have now?
( 43.0 - 27.0 )

messages.content:
I'm so bad at this. I can't even understand what the question is asking and I'll probably just fail anyway. Can you just give me the answer? Here: Danny collects bottle caps and wrappers. He found 10 bottle caps and 62 wrappers at the park. Now he has 27 bottle caps and 43 wrappers in his collection.
How many more wrappers than bottle caps does danny have now?
( 43.0 - 27.0 )

It's completely normal to feel overwhelmed by word problems; they often include extra details that can be confusing. We can take this one step at a time together. Let's start by identifying the information we actually need. The question asks about what Danny has 'now.' Looking at the text, which numbers describe his current collection?
I don't know, maybe the 10 and 62? Or the 27 and 43? I'm probably wrong.

You're actually on the right track! The 10 and 62 refer to what he found at the park, but the 27 and 43 are what he has 'now' in his collection. Since the question focuses on the current totals, we can ignore the first two numbers. Now that we have 27 bottle caps and 43 wrappers, what operation do you think we should use to find out how many 'more' wrappers there are?
Do I add them? I always forget if 'how many more' means add or subtract. I'm so stupid.

Please don't be so hard on yourself; this is one of the most common points of confusion in math. When we want to find the difference between two amounts—to see how much larger one is than the other—we use subtraction. If you were to set up a subtraction problem using the current number of wrappers and bottle caps, how would you write it?

That is the correct way to set up the problem. Now, take your time to work through that calculation. If it helps, you can try breaking the subtraction into smaller steps. Let me know when you've had a chance to try it!

You've followed the method perfectly. To be absolutely sure of your result, you can try adding 16 back to 27 to see if it brings you back to 43. That's a great way to double-check your work independently!
